questions.title: Example Functions

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The shape, executed:

```go
func ExampleDouble() {
    fmt.Println(double(21))
    // Output: 42
}
```

go test runs it: double(21) prints 42; the Output: comment says 42 — PASS (verified in our test module).

The doc relationship: Example functions become documentation — pkg.go.dev shows them alongside the function they demonstrate (ExampleDouble documents Double by example). The reader sees the call AND the expected output — and it's TESTED: change double()'s behavior and the Example fails — the docs can't rot.

The naming convention: Example + the function name (ExampleDouble documents Double). Variants: ExampleDouble_negative — a named suffix; ExampleDoubleSuite if the function is in a different position.

The Output comment rules: the exact expected stdout (leading/trailing whitespace matches; blank lines separate multiple outputs). No Output comment = the Example runs but isn't verified (still useful as doc).

The discipline: Examples ARE the API's usage spec — write them for anything users will call, and they double as the tutorial. The standard library is full of them — the stdlib docs ARE Examples.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    E[ExampleDouble] --> R[run fn body]
    R --> CAP[capture stdout]
    CAP --> CMP{== Output: comment?}
    CMP -->|yes| P[PASS — doc is correct]
    CMP -->|no| F[FAIL — doc has drifted]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanism: the test framework compiles Example functions, captures their stdout (redirecting os.Stdout for the duration), and compares — exact match against the Output: comment. The comparison is string-equality on the captured output, which makes Examples deterministic-only — no time, no random, no network output.

The doc-site integration: pkg.go.dev and godoc extract the Example's source (the body) and the Output comment, rendering them as the function's example section. The Example is tested code that becomes documentation without any additional step — the single-source-of-truth documentation pattern.

The relation to the other test types: Example functions are the ONLY test form that's both executable AND rendered — Test functions are internal assertions; Examples are the public-facing documentation that the test suite verifies. Together with table-driven tests, they're the Go community's answer to 'documentation that lies' — the doc can't drift because it fails the test when it does.
